title: The princes of Persia and Greece and Michael (Dan 10:13, 20–21)
speaker: The man clothed in linen
description: A heavenly conflict: the prince of Persia resists, Michael helps, and the prince of Greece "will come". The chapter introduces the revelation of 11:2–12:4.
in_text_interpretation: Michael is "your prince" — the prince of Daniel's people (10:21; 12:1). The princes of Persia and Greece are not otherwise identified.

interpretations.label: Patron (guardian) angels of the nations
proponents: Jerome (citing Deut 32:8: "according to the number of the angels of God")
interpretations.summary: Each nation has an angelic prince in heaven whose success matches its own; Michael is Israel's. Textual reasoning: Deut 32:8 in the LXX (and a reading Driver notes some think original) divides the nations "according to the number of the sons/angels of God"; Sir 17:17; Isa 24:21. Driver: the doctrine of tutelary angels appears distinctly for the first time here, developed later into seventy angel-princes of the nations (Targum Ps.-Jonathan, as cited by Driver). This is a statement about the text's worldview, not a historical claim.

interpretations.label: Hostile spiritual powers (high-ranking demons) opposing God's purposes
proponents: D. Guzik (citing Walvoord, Wood and Baldwin)
interpretations.summary: The prince of Persia is "a demon of high rank", not a human ruler; prayer is linked to unseen conflict (cf. Eph 6:12; John 12:31). Guzik rejects reading the prince as a human king.

interpretations.label: The coming of the prince of Greece = the Macedonian overthrow of Persia
interpretations.summary: After the Jews were freed, Alexander slew Darius and overthrew the Persians and Medes, so that "the prince of the Greeks did overcome the prince of the Persians". Historical evidence: Arrian on Gaugamela (331) and Darius III's death (330). Objection: the text speaks of heavenly princes, and the link to a particular event is the interpreter's.

referents.referent: The rise of Alexander's Macedon against Persia
